name: Wendy Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We are independent of employers, AI firms, unions and government, and your answers are confidential. What does your usual day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 27, with a master’s degree and a chartered accountancy qualification, and I lead reviews of accounts and tax returns at an accounting firm. I am good at finding a missing invoice in a client’s file, and I like sending out a return I can explain line by line. I have never used an AI tool; I trust the process I know. Chasing the same missing paperwork twice is the part that wears me down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the household side of the picture?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live alone, earn the usual salary for this job and have around four months of expenses saved. There are some similar jobs nearby, but I would rather keep this one. I am fairly middle-of-the-road on politics and cautious about risky changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say our tax returns still need careful checking, whatever small shortcuts the software offers. Clients do not pay for a colourful dashboard; they pay us to get the figures right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have about four months of expenses saved and earn normal pay for this work, so a minor change does not scare me. I would rather keep the methods I trust than test a tool on someone’s tax bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep my paper checklist beside each digital account file and review the team’s returns as usual. In the first year I would ask the manager to show me any new routine check before it becomes part of our sign-off, but I would not use an AI tool myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my own pay and schedule. The small software changes sound like another office rule to learn, nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you keep the paper list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I once found a missed invoice because I had written a little box for it. The list lets me see where I stopped when a client calls halfway through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the manager makes the new check compulsory?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a walk-through using an old file and write down each step. I can follow a checked process without wanting to experiment with a new tool.

say: I would say clients pay for **correct tax figures**, not a new dashboard.
I would keep the **sign-off check** clear before accepting small shortcuts.
think: My **four-month cushion** and ordinary pay leave me secure in a mild change.
I trust my **paper checklist** more than an untested AI tool.
do: Keep reviewing **tax returns** against my paper checklist.
Ask for a **walk-through** before any compulsory routine check joins sign-off.
feel: I feel **calm** about my own pay and schedule.
S0.quote: Clients do not pay for a colourful dashboard; they pay us to get the figures right.
fieldNote: Her **paper checklist** is a practical memory aid built from a past invoice error, not just a symbol of resistance.
She would accept a **compulsory check** after a walk-through, but has never used AI tools and does not volunteer to experiment.

steps.text: Keep reviewing client tax returns against paper checklist

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the firm that every automated check needs a named person who owns the final return. If junior posts disappear, senior accountants will inherit both the files and the blame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tax writing and checking take most of my day, so I can see the firm needing fewer hours even from me. Four months saved and some other local firms give me time to look, but I do not want to restart somewhere strange.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask my manager for a list of which checks will move to software and whether my hours stay the same. I would keep doing the existing review work; if a cut is announced in the first year, I would update my CV and apply only to advertised senior-accountant posts nearby while staying employed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about hours, though I can pay bills for a while if I have to. I dislike the idea of being handed errors from a process I did not choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the first sign your own hours are at risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A notice that we will not replace a reviewer, followed by fewer files coming to me. I would ask for the actual hours forecast rather than guess from gossip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take an AI course to keep the role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take a required, paid walk-through of our firm’s approved system, but I would not pay for a speculative course myself. I need to see the job requirement in writing first.

say: I would require a **named reviewer** for every automated tax check.
I would warn that shrinking **junior staffing** loads more files onto senior accountants.
think: My **writing and checking** hours could shrink as software takes those tasks.
I have **four months saved**, but starting over at another firm worries me.
do: Request a **written hours forecast**; take a paid approved-system walk-through only if the job requirement is written.
Keep doing **current reviews** while hours remain.
Apply to **advertised local senior posts** after a cut is announced, without resigning first.
feel: I feel **anxious** about reduced hours and unfamiliar new work.
S1.quote: I dislike the idea of being handed errors from a process I did not choose.
fieldNote: Her **resistance** is focused on accountability: she wants a named person and a documented process before changes reach client returns.
She has **some local alternatives**, yet will start an external search only after an announced cut and while keeping her present pay.

steps.text: Keep reviewing tax files while existing hours remain
Apply to advertised nearby senior-accountant posts after announced hours cut
Take paid approved-system walkthrough only after written job requirement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2028 means a machine could do most thinking work in accounts and tax returns by 2028. The hands-on robots around 2031 are not the date our office should plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am one of the better reviewers here, but I expect the firm to remove my post once cheaper AGI can do nearly all this thinking work. Four months of savings will cover bills briefly, and I do not know whether nearby firms will still have senior openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask for a written notice period and a clear list of which client work stays with people. I would stop the monthly weekend train trip to preserve cash; in the first year after 2028, if my hours are cut, I would apply to every advertised local accounting vacancy and ask my parents for a temporary room only if the savings drop below one month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed and wakeful about the rent. I cannot make myself believe that being careful is enough when the whole task may be cheaper elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would explain the hours cut and show them my remaining savings before asking for the room. I would set a three-month limit and keep paying my share of food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you switch to a different trade immediately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would first try the accounting vacancies because my master’s and chartered qualification are what I have built. If there are no openings, I would ask a local careers office about paid retraining before enrolling in anything.

say: I would say **AGI by 2028** reaches our tax desks before capable robots arrive.
I would demand **written notice** before the firm cuts hours.
think: I expect the firm to remove my **desk post** after AGI arrives.
My **four-month cushion** could run out before nearby firms hire again.
do: Ask for a **written notice period** and a list of human client work.
Stop the **monthly train trip** now to preserve cash.
Apply for **advertised accounting vacancies** after lost hours; seek a parents’ room below one month of savings.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about losing rent money despite a short buffer.
S2.quote: I cannot make myself believe that being careful is enough when the whole task may be cheaper elsewhere.
fieldNote: The **2031 robot date** offers no shelter because her tax and accounts reviews are screen-based thinking work.
Her **fallback** is to cut travel, search after lost hours, and ask her parents for a room below one month saved.

steps.text: Stop monthly weekend train trip to preserve savings
Apply to advertised accounting vacancies after hours are cut
Ask parents for temporary room if savings fall below one month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my team AGI by 2031 gives us a few years to set rules for who checks the returns. I would want the firm to show a real staffing timetable, not an inspirational memo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years might be enough to build a larger cushion and learn a new part of accounting, but I still expect my desk work to shrink in 2031. The robots in 2034 are a later question for other workplaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask to observe tax dispute meetings once a month, where I can see whether clients still value an accountant speaking for them. I would save 75 a month if my hours and usual pay hold; in the first year after 2031 I would take a paid disputes vacancy at this firm only with written salary and hours, or keep my current reviews while applying for an advertised local post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but I can picture a calendar with five years on it. I would still worry that a dispute role could turn into unpaid extra work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you look for in a dispute meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would listen for questions clients cannot answer from the software printout. If the firm charges for that advice and protects the accountant’s time, it might be a real job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a course now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a short course only after the meetings show paid demand. I would enroll if the firm confirms fees and paid study hours in writing; I will not use my emergency savings to pay for a tax disputes course.

say: I would ask for a **staffing timetable** and clear checking rules before 2031.
I would tell colleagues the **2034 robots** do not delay office changes.
think: My **desk work** can shrink in 2031 even with years to prepare.
I could build a **larger cushion** if ordinary pay holds.
do: Observe **monthly tax disputes** to test whether clients pay for advice.
Save **75 monthly** if current hours and pay hold.
Enroll in a **disputes course** only after meetings show paid demand and written fees and paid study hours are approved.
feel: I feel **anxious**, although five years gives me a workable calendar.
S3.quote: I will not use my emergency savings to pay for a tax disputes course.
fieldNote: Her **monthly observation** is a way to test actual paid demand before taking a course or changing roles.
Written **fees and hours** matter because she will not trade her emergency cushion for a vague new title.

steps.text: Enroll in disputes course after paid demand and written employer fee and paid-time approval
Save 75 monthly if current hours and pay hold
Take paid disputes vacancy with written salary and hours or apply to advertised local post

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2036 gives the firm time to plan staff changes without springing them on people. I would ask for clear rules about who signs client returns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years could let me build a bigger reserve and keep doing work I know for a while. I might be 37 when AGI reaches these screens, and a good title will not protect me if the work itself moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep leading reviews and ask for one client dispute meeting each quarter, to see whether I can do that part well. I would save 100 a month while my hours and usual pay hold; in the first year after 2036 I would remain in a paid client-facing post only if the salary and hours are written down, otherwise apply for advertised nearby accounting posts before resigning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the distant change, but my current job and income look sound over the next few years. A decade feels like enough time to make careful choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge whether you can do dispute work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the partner to tell me what I missed after each meeting and note whether the client paid for the advice. I am willing to learn from a real case, not a sales pitch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move away for a role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would look at local firms first because there are some, and I like my current home. I would consider a move only with an actual offer and written pay high enough to cover higher rent.

say: I would ask for **clear sign-off rules** as the firm plans toward 2036.
I would support **advance staff notice** rather than surprise changes.
think: A **good title** will not protect me if review work moves to AGI.
Ten years may let me build a **larger reserve** while pay holds.
do: Keep **leading reviews** and observe one client dispute meeting quarterly.
Save **100 monthly** while current hours and pay hold.
Keep a **paid client-facing post** only with written salary and hours; otherwise apply nearby while employed.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about 2036 while my nearer-term income looks sound.
S4.quote: A decade feels like enough time to make careful choices.
fieldNote: The **long runway** suits her cautious style: she tests dispute work in quarterly meetings and keeps current reviews.
She sets **written salary and hours** for any later client-facing post, while savings depend on her existing hours and pay.

steps.text: Keep leading reviews and observe quarterly client dispute meetings
Save 100 monthly while current hours and pay hold
Keep client-facing post with written salary and hours or apply nearby before resigning

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because almost all my work is on a screen and the firm might cut hours quickly. Honest notice, actual local vacancies and a temporary place with my parents would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask how long it takes to trust a new checking process. My paper checklist is a map of mistakes I have already seen, not a fear of screens.

headlineQuote: My paper checklist is a map of mistakes I have already seen, not a fear of screens.
portrait: At **27**, Wendy leads account and tax reviews with a master’s degree and chartered accountancy qualification.
She has **typical pay**, four months of expenses saved and some similar jobs nearby.
She has **never used AI** and prefers her tested paper checklist, though she will learn a required process through a walk-through.
The **2028 scenario** alarms her; longer lead times let her observe dispute work and save while keeping present hours.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her screen-based review work before she finds another accounting post.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **honest notice**, actual local vacancies and temporary housing from her parents if savings run low.
